question: How does fire spread on fabric in microgravity?
answer:
In microgravity, when a thin fuel is ignited in the middle at low forced-flow velocities, the flame spreads upstream into the oncoming airflow [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Airflow along fabric surfaces, including Nomex and 75% cotton with 25% fiberglass blends measuring 1 to 2 cm, can be applied in opposed or concurrent directions at speeds up to 40 cm/s [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80]. Results from the BASS experiment indicate that materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Testing aboard the International Space Station has included 122 experimental test rows evaluating flame size, shape, color, and spread rate [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80]. 

The provided sources do not cover specific numerical values for flame spread rates on fabric in microgravity.

question: Which experiments tested oxygen levels above 30%?
answer:
Based on the NASA PSI data, four experiments tested oxygen levels above 30% [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row]:

- PSI-159 ACME CFI-G tested oxygen levels from 12% to 85% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-159 · doi:10.60555/cyt1-kh64].
- PSI-10 ACME/Flame Design tested oxygen levels from 19.8048% to 84.9978% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-10 · doi:10.60555/w4zy-bt45].
- PSI-20 ACME BRE tested oxygen levels from 21% to 40% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-20 · doi:10.60555/vb93-3y72].
- PSI-69 FLEX tested oxygen levels from 12% to 34% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row].

question: How was smoke detection tested on the ISS, and why does it matter?
answer:
Smoke detection was tested on the ISS through experiments such as the Dust Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test, which measured background particulate levels, and the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. The SAME experiment evaluated solid fuels including Teflon, Kapton, Silicone Rubber, Lampwick, and Dibutyl Phthalate under airflow speeds of 5–10 cm/s across 8 experimental test rows using smoke detectors, video cameras, thermophoretic soot samplers, and a Transmission Electron microscope [PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62]. 

This testing matters because reduced gravity causes smoke particles to grow larger than in normal gravity, which alters detector responses and could cause terrestrial detectors to miss microgravity fires [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62]. Gathering this reduced-gravity baseline data enables engineers to create reliable, sensitive fire detection systems for long-duration spaceflight as well as extreme Earth environments like submarines [PSI-101 · doi:10.60555/2np7-jv14][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62][PSI-47 · doi:10.60555/ztgj-d202].

question: What gases were used to put out flames, and in which experiment?
answer: Nitrogen gas was used for extinguishment in a drop tower test burning a PMMA sphere [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Nitrogen was also applied to flames as a suppressant in early results [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Additionally, in the FLEX experiment, a droplet flame was tested in an atmosphere containing carbon dioxide and nitrogen [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. The FLEX investigation also planned to test gaseous suppressants such as carbon dioxide, helium, and SF6 [PSI-69 · doi:10.60555/mbq8-0451]. The sources do not cover which specific gases were used in the BASS experiment, stating only that an inert gaseous agent was planned to be assessed [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80].

question: What happened in the Mir fire in 1997, and what was learned?
answer:
On Feb. 24, 1997, a fire ignited in a solid fuel oxygen generator in the Kvant-1 module aboard the Mir space station [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. The searing flame lasted several minutes, blocked access to one of two Soyuz escape vehicles, and filled the modules with toxic smoke [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. Through teamwork, the six crew members extinguished the fire without structural damage or lasting harm, and life support cleared the atmosphere over several hours [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. 

Following the incident, Russian space officials updated emergency crew training, ground controller emergency responses, and the ground preparation of oxygen canisters [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. Lessons were also passed on to the design and operations of the International Space Station, which implemented a robust oxygen generation system with dissimilar redundancies and added safety measures for backup solid fuel oxygen generators [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir].

question: Is there any fire data for Moon or Mars gravity?
answer:
The NASA Physical Science Informatics (PSI) repository contains zero investigations conducted in real Moon or Mars gravity [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion]. Out of 24 PSI investigations, 23 studied microgravity and one (PSI-22) used an electric field to mimic partial gravity [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion]. Terrestrial testing has simulated lunar gravity using a drop tower centrifuge to observe fabric burning in air [NASA Combustion Science · nasa.gov/glenn/glenn-expertise-space-exploration/physical-sciences-program/combustion-science]. The Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment is planned to be performed on the Moon to investigate material flammability in reduced gravity [NASA Combustion Science · nasa.gov/glenn/glenn-expertise-space-exploration/physical-sciences-program/combustion-science]. In low-flow partial gravity conditions, some materials are flammable at lower oxygen concentrations than in normal gravity [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. 

Our sources do not cover any fire data directly gathered on the surface of Mars [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion].

question: What are cool flames and why are they a risk?
answer:
Cool flames are a low-temperature combustion regime marked by very weak flames with peak temperatures between 500 and 1000 K [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-159 · doi:10.60555/cyt1-kh64]. They form as an intermediate step between unreacted fuel and oxidizer and can burn for a prolonged period after a visible flame extinguishes [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. During droplet combustion, cool flames burn only a fraction of the vaporized fuel, leaving behind a fuel vapor cloud [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science].

Cool flames are a risk because reduced-gravity environments are particularly conducive to low-temperature combustion, creating spacecraft fire safety concerns [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Improving the understanding of cool flame reactivity helps support the design of safer spacecraft systems [PSI-39 · doi:10.60555/m6pj-a914].

The provided sources do not fully cover specific terrestrial risk mechanisms or detailed hazards beyond spacecraft fire safety concerns and fuel vapor cloud formation [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-39 · doi:10.60555/m6pj-a914].
